title: A better question, first
summary: A practical notebook for separating evidence, interpretation, and uncertainty.
question: What would change your mind?

sections.heading: Frame a question you can investigate
paragraphs: This sample note describes an editorial process rather than a trading strategy. A useful research question is narrow enough to investigate and open enough to admit an unwelcome answer.
Write the question before collecting material. Then keep a record of why it matters, what evidence would be relevant, and what you cannot yet know.
prompts: What is the question, in one sentence?
What evidence would support a different explanation?
When should this question be revisited?

sections.heading: Separate three layers
paragraphs: Use distinct notes for observations, interpretations, and unresolved questions. An observation records what a source says. An interpretation explains what you think it means. An open question marks the limits of that interpretation.
This separation gives future readers a way to inspect the reasoning, and gives you a way to revise it without rewriting the history of the decision.

sections.heading: Leave a useful trail
paragraphs: Keep source links, dates, and short explanations of material changes. A concise research log can be more useful than a polished conclusion that hides how it was reached.
Close the note with the next piece of evidence to look for. The aim is not to make every uncertainty disappear, but to make the remaining work clear.
